open-question.question: Where is the banner SVG committed, and how does it reach the three host landing pages, given that a host README's relative path resolves only to a file its own host tree carries and that the build copies only the root LICENSE into every tree: is a copy carried in each host tree and referenced by a relative path, or do the host READMEs reference a single file in the source repository by absolute URL? If each tree carries a copy, where does it come from: a file kept by hand in each of the three definition directories under scripts/hosts/, or a build change that copies one shared file into every tree?

What is the source of truth for the banner: is the SVG file written and edited directly, or is the character art kept as a plain-text drawing from which a committed script generates the SVG, the repository holding no such script today?
open-question.alternative: The committed SVG is the only source of truth. It is written and later edited by hand as SVG, with the character art, its colours, and its layout held only inside the file. No plain-text drawing is kept beside it and no generator script is committed. However its first version comes to be written, every later change is an edit of the SVG itself. One artifact and nothing to keep in step with it. The repository gains no script, no new dependency, and no command a later editor must know to run. This matches how the README templates and the three traffic-workflow copies are kept today, as hand-edited files. Changing the art means editing XML: positions, row elements, and characters that must be escaped (a literal & or < in the art becomes an entity). A diff of the art is then unreadable as a picture, so a reviewer cannot see what a change does to the drawing. Whether direct editing is practical at all depends on the Character rendering in SVG question's axis: with text elements it is tedious, and with glyphs converted to outline paths it is effectively impossible by hand.

A plain-text drawing of the arms, with whatever colour mapping it needs, is committed as the source of truth. A new standalone script under scripts/ is committed beside it, run by hand like set_version.py, and reads the drawing to write the SVG. The generated SVG is committed as derived output, never hand-edited, and is regenerated whenever the drawing changes. The art stays editable and reviewable as a picture in plain text, and the SVG is reproducible from it. A redraw, a palette change, or a switch in how the characters are rendered is one edit plus one rerun, not a rewrite of the XML. Generated output that is committed and never hand-edited is the pattern the repository already follows for hosts/. The repository gains a script that must be written, kept working, and remembered whenever the art changes. Nothing ties the committed SVG to the drawing, so the two can drift silently unless a guard is added. Whether such a guard exists is the Permanent banner check question's axis, not this one's. The script also has to take a position on the Character rendering in SVG and Light and dark themes questions' axes, which becomes code to change if either answer changes.

alternative.id: Drawing rendered by the host build

open-question.alternative: The plain-text drawing is committed as the source of truth, and scripts/build_hosts.py itself renders the SVG from it as part of every host build. The generated file is written into each host tree and committed there as build output, with --check comparing it against a fresh render like every other file in the tree. The root README's copy is produced by the same rendering code rather than by a separate script. The drawing and the host copies of the SVG cannot drift unnoticed: the existing --check gate catches any difference on every push, in CI, and in the release pre-flight. There is no separate command for anyone to remember to run. Banner-specific rendering moves into the one generic host build, which today renders templates and has no host-specific or content-specific code. The build writes nothing outside hosts/, so the root README's copy falls outside --check unless the build's output set is widened. This option only works if the Banner delivery to host pages question has each host tree carry its own copy, rather than having the READMEs reference one file by absolute URL.

The plain-text drawing is committed beside the SVG as a readable reference to the art. The SVG is produced from it once, by hand or by a one-off conversion that is not committed. From then on the SVG is the file the READMEs use, and a later change is made to both by hand. No generator script lives in the repository. Reviewers can read the art as text in the repository and in diffs, and no script has to be maintained. Two hand-kept artifacts describe one picture with no mechanical link between them, so they drift as soon as one is edited without the other. The SVG is then the real source of truth in practice, and the text file a record that may already be out of date. A redraw also means repeating or reconstructing the conversion that was never kept.

open-question.question: How are the banner's characters drawn inside the SVG, given that GitHub loads no external font for an SVG shown as an image and a text element is drawn in whatever font the viewer's system supplies: as text elements relying on a system monospace font stack, as text with a font embedded in the file, or as glyph outlines converted to paths?
Which characters may the banner's art use: only the printable 7-bit ASCII characters, or also Unicode characters such as box-drawing, block, or braille glyphs?
open-question.alternative: The art uses only the 95 printable 7-bit ASCII characters (U+0020 to U+007E): the arms' curls are built from characters such as / \ | ( ) _ ~ ' . , o and similar, and no character outside that range appears anywhere in the drawing. It keeps the goal's "ASCII art" literal, and every monospace font a viewer's system can supply covers this range with one uniform advance width, so the columns stay aligned and no glyph falls back to a different font whichever way the characters end up drawn in the SVG; the drawing also stays a plain-text file any editor or script handles without encoding concerns. Curves made of slashes, brackets, and underscores are coarse and stair-stepped, so arms curling up from the bottom edge read less smoothly and need more columns and rows to look organic, and the colour palette can only tint thin line characters, with no solid or shaded areas to carry it.

alternative.id: ASCII plus box-drawing and block glyphs

open-question.alternative: The art may use the printable ASCII characters plus the Unicode Box Drawing (U+2500 to U+257F) and Block Elements (U+2580 to U+259F) ranges, for example rounded arcs such as ╭ ╮ ╰ ╯, lines, and the shade and fill blocks ░ ▒ ▓ █; braille and every other Unicode range stay excluded. Rounded arc glyphs give the curling arms smooth turns that slashes cannot, and the shade blocks let the violet and grey-blue palette fill and grade the arms' bodies, while both ranges are carried by the common monospace fonts (Menlo, Consolas, DejaVu Sans Mono and the like) at the same cell width as ASCII. The art is no longer ASCII in the strict sense the goal's wording names, and its alignment holds only where the glyphs are drawn at a uniform width: whether that is guaranteed depends on the sibling question of how the characters are rendered in the SVG, since a viewer font lacking a glyph substitutes another font whose width and baseline may differ, and block glyphs can show hairline seams between rows.

The art may use any Unicode character the drawing calls for, braille patterns (U+2800 to U+28FF) included alongside ASCII, box-drawing, and block glyphs, with no range excluded. Braille patterns give each character cell a 2 by 4 grid of dots, so the arms' curves and suckers can be drawn at close to pixel resolution, giving the smoothest and most detailed silhouette any character set allows. Braille and the less common ranges have the weakest monospace font coverage, so this option is viable only if the sibling question on character rendering settles on a method that does not depend on the viewer's fonts; dense braille also reads as a dithered picture rather than as a drawing made of characters, drifting furthest from the "ASCII art" the goal names, and the plain-text source becomes hard to read or edit by hand.

open-question.question: How does the banner handle GitHub's light and dark page themes, no README today using a picture element or a theme-specific image variant: one image with a transparent background whose colours must read on both page backgrounds, one image with its own filled background, or separate light and dark variants selected per theme?

Which exact colour values make up the banner's violet and grey-blue palette: the values the root README's workflow diagram already uses (violet #9333ea and #581c87, slate #94a3b8 and #475569), or values chosen for the banner alone?
How many arms does the banner show, the goal saying only "several": all eight of an octopus's arms, or a smaller number?
open-question.alternative: The banner shows exactly eight arms, every one of an octopus's arms, each curling up from the bottom edge, and the requirements record eight as a fixed count the drawing must meet. It carries the image the project already chose: ideas/gurita.md records that an octopus has eight arms and that "the plugin is the arms", so the banner states the full metaphor rather than a fragment of it, and a fixed count gives the drawing an objective criterion to be checked against. Eight curling arms side by side need many character columns to stay legible, so the art is either wide or crowded with arms too thin to curl; whether that fits depends on the column count and display width the banner-size question settles, and an eight-arm drawing is the hardest of the options to make read well in characters.

The banner shows a fixed number of arms below eight, chosen from three to five, framed as a view in which only some of the octopus's arms rise into the banner, and the requirements record the exact number the drawing must meet. Fewer arms leave each one room for a full, legible curl within a modest width, the reading the goal's "several" already suggests, while a recorded number still gives the drawing an objective criterion. It gives up the eight-arm image the naming draft rests on, so a viewer reads it as part of an octopus rather than the whole set of arms the plugin claims to be, and any number chosen in the range is arbitrary with no project fact to anchor it.

No arm count is recorded: the requirements keep the goal's "several", meaning more than two, and the number is settled when the character drawing is made, by whatever look reads best at the banner's size. The count follows from the drawing's actual space and legibility rather than being fixed before any art exists, so it never forces eight arms into too few columns or leaves an awkward gap with too few. The drawing has no countable criterion to be accepted against, so the number becomes whatever the drawer's judgment yields; that is acceptable only as far as the drawing-author-and-approval question puts a judge in place who can weigh it, and an unattended drawer may land on a count that reads as neither a deliberate eight nor a deliberate fragment.

open-question.question: What size is the banner, given that it sits above everything else on the page and pushes the badges and title down: how many character columns and rows does the art occupy, and at what width is the image displayed, the full width of the README column or a fixed narrower width?

Who produces the character drawing of the arms, and what decides it is good enough to ship: does the executing agent draw it and accept it on its own judgment against criteria recorded in the requirements, does the agent draw it for the maintainer to approve before it lands in the READMEs, or does the maintainer supply the drawing?

How is the banner's rendered appearance checked before it is committed, the repository holding no tool that renders an SVG: by rendering the file locally to an image that is inspected, by viewing it on GitHub after a push in both page themes, or by no rendering check beyond the file being a well-formed SVG?
What alternative text does the banner image carry in the four READMEs: an empty alt marking the image as decorative, or a short description of the arms, and in that case what wording?

Does this mission include a release that publishes the banner to the three host landing pages, which change only when a release publishes the host trees, or does it end with the banner committed on main, showing only on the source repository's page until the next release?

Is the host suite run on all three hosts as part of this mission, since adding the banner to each host's README template changes every host's trigger set and the suite first requires each host's installed copy to equal the built tree, or is that run left to the next release's pre-flight?

Does a permanent check guard the banner once it is in place, for example a test that each of the four READMEs opens with the banner image or that every committed copy of the SVG is identical, or is the banner verified once when its tasks are completed, no test reading a README's content today?
